source: Zhu and Simon (1987) Learning mathematics from examples and by doing (CMU technical report AIP-4 version)
finding: First big classroom programme on learning algebra from worked-out examples with no lecture. Experiment 1 taught factoring of quadratics (x2+ax+b) to about 13-year-old first-year algebra pupils in Beijing. No pupil could solve the pretest problems. After the review of prerequisites and a few examples and problems, almost all could solve the test.
numbers: Classroom: 98 pupils, 4 excluded for passing the pretest, so 94. 78 (83%) solved all 5 test problems, 8 (8.5%) solved 3, 8 (8.5%) solved 2 or fewer, within one class session. Protocol group: 20 pupils, 10 with worked examples (E) and 10 with a carefully ordered problem sequence only (D). After about 25 minutes all 20 solved the test problems and 15 of 20 answered the procedure questions.
quote: no comparison was made with a control group using conventional learning methods
limits: Experiment 1 had no conventional control group, so it shows feasibility, not superiority. The 1987 report is a tech report; the journal version may differ. Small protocol samples.
agent_relevance: Shows the paradigm: a short, ordered run of solved cases lets a novice induce a rule. A subgoal library seeded with ordered solved cases is the agent analogue.

source: Zhu and Simon (1987) Learning mathematics from examples and by doing (CMU technical report AIP-4 version)
finding: Worked-example group beat a lecture control in one school and tied it in another on the same factoring task.
numbers: School A: 32 pupils per condition, post-test 93.13% (examples) vs 75.50% (control), p<.001 by t-test; learning time about 40 minutes in both, control slightly (ns) longer. School B: 39 vs 38 pupils, 97.23% vs 95.08%, not significant; no time difference (about 30 minutes).
limits: Own replication on the same task gave a large gain in one school and a null in the other. Control teaching quality is not described in this report. Pupils not randomly assigned individually (classroom design).
agent_relevance: The effect size depends on how strong the baseline is. Expect small gains where the plain agent already does well.

source: Zhu and Simon (1987) Learning mathematics from examples and by doing (CMU technical report AIP-4 version)
finding: Exponent laws: example-based instruction scored higher than control on all three laws and took less time.
numbers: First run: 32 of 36 pupils (89%) scored 80% or more on law 1; all 36 on law 2; 21 of 35 on law 3 (all 35 at 60% or more). 1985 replication with control: example group 93.1, 95.4 and 90.2 on the three laws; mixed tasks 88 vs 73.1 for control. Time 180 minutes vs 270 minutes for control. Significant at .05 and .001 only for laws 2 and 3.
limits: Per-group Ns for the 1985 control comparison are not given in the report. Tests are reported as school scores, not item-level.
agent_relevance: A time saving of about one third at equal or better score is the pattern the effect usually shows: efficiency more than accuracy.

source: Zhu and Simon (1987) Learning mathematics from examples and by doing (CMU technical report AIP-4 version)
finding: Geometry proofs: gains were small and not always significant. Material redesign after the first two schools raised scores. Time savings were larger than score gains.
numbers: 1984, four schools, example-group means 76.9, 77.9, 89.1 and 83.5%. School M: 89.1 vs 85.2% (ns), pupils reaching the skill 94.6 vs 88% (significant), time 50 vs 75 min. School N: 83.5 vs 83.2% (ns), skill 90.6 vs 85%, time 50 vs 70 min. 1985 one-school replication: 89 vs 83% (ns at .05), same class time of 50 min but the control spent 20 more minutes on homework.
limits: Mostly non-significant on score. The authors call the differences generally modest. The material was changed between schools, so the schools are not pure replications.
agent_relevance: Matches the later finding that geometry-type examples need good layout (see split attention). Material design matters as much as having examples.

source: Zhu and Simon (1987) Learning mathematics from examples and by doing (CMU technical report AIP-4 version)
finding: One-year retention was good for both groups, slightly better for example learners. A full three-year Chinese middle-school course was compressed into two years with example-based materials, but the authors warn this does not prove the method caused the saving.
numbers: Factoring: example class 97.2 (1984) then 96.0 (1985); control 95.0 then 92.1. Geometry: example class 89.1 then 96.3; control 85.2 then 86.7. Full course: one average Beijing class finished 2 years of algebra plus 1 year of geometry in 2 years; the authors say a one-third saving, if confirmed, needs caution.
quote: the differences in success ... were generally modest in magnitude, they were positive
limits: Single class for the full course, no randomisation, test scores not yet analysed at time of report. The 'one third' figure is the authors' hedged projection. Later reviews repeat the 3-in-2-years story without the hedge.
agent_relevance: Do not repeat the '3 years in 2' claim as a result. Use it only as an anecdote.

source: Zhu and Simon (1987) Learning mathematics from examples and by doing (CMU technical report AIP-4 version)
finding: A production-system account of learning from examples. Pupils compare the unfactored and factored forms, notice what changed (the factors add to the linear coefficient and multiply to the constant), and turn that into a condition-action rule. Later examples split the rule into sign cases. Pupils learned about five productions and could mostly state them.
numbers: Protocols: 9 of 10 example pupils and 8 of 9 'doing' pupils could state the rule when asked (one doing protocol was lost). About 5 productions acquired per pupil.
limits: Verbal-protocol evidence on 19 pupils in one task. The model is descriptive. It is not a fitted simulation.
agent_relevance: A direct template for a library entry: condition (pattern seen in the example), action (step), plus the sign-case split. Entries are induced from contrast between before and after states.

source: Sweller, van Merrienboer and Paas (1998) Cognitive architecture and instructional design
finding: Theory statement of the worked-example effect. Solving by means-ends analysis loads working memory with the goal, the current state and the difference between them, which leaves little capacity to build schemas. A worked example removes the search and focuses attention on problem states and the operators that move between them, so extraneous load is low. The paper calls the prediction counterintuitive: studying examples can beat solving the same problems.
numbers: Sets out the architecture; no new experiment. Cites the series Sweller and Cooper 1985; Cooper and Sweller 1987; Zhu and Simon 1987 (3-year course in 2 years).
limits: A review by the theory's authors. It treats the load claim as established; direct load measures come only from some cited studies (Paas 1992 and later).
agent_relevance: Maps to a no-search mode: give the agent the solved path and the operators, not a goal to search toward. Supports using stored solved cases before letting the agent try.

source: Sweller, van Merrienboer and Paas (1998) Cognitive architecture and instructional design
finding: Review of the core worked-example experiments. Algebra studies show better schema construction and new-problem solving. Paas 1992 (statistics) gave a worked example to conventional learners only after they failed; they still did worse than a worked-example group, which the authors explain by failed solutions entering the schema. Paas and van Merrienboer 1994a used a pure worked condition (study only) in geometry.
numbers: Paas and van Merrienboer 1994a: pure worked condition had lower extraneous load scores, better schema construction, higher transfer and better instructional efficiency than the conventional condition. Trafton and Reiser 1993 (LISP) and Carroll 1994 (remedial maths, English-to-equation translation) also favour examples. Exact means are not given in the review.
limits: Secondary report; effect sizes absent.
agent_relevance: Order matters: letting the agent fail first and then see the answer may bake the failed path into memory. Store the clean solution, not the failure trail.

source: Sweller, van Merrienboer and Paas (1998) Cognitive architecture and instructional design
finding: Costs and limits of heavy worked-example use: possible loss of motivation without real problem solving, stereotyped patterns that hinder creative solutions (Smith, Ward and Schumacher 1993), and load from poor design (split sources, redundancy, low-variability sets). Completion problems (partial solution, learner finishes it) are proposed as the bridge from worked examples to conventional problems.
numbers: Completion strategy: worked example = completion problem with full solution; conventional problem = completion problem with no solution. Programming studies cited (van Merrienboer 1990; van Merrienboer and de Croock 1989) found higher construction scores with completion assignments than with conventional assignments.
limits: No effect sizes in the review. Fixation claim rests on a design-fixation study, not on worked-example experiments.
agent_relevance: Pair with a fixation guard: a library of solved cases can narrow the search. Fading from full solution to partial gives a built-in schedule.

source: Sweller, van Merrienboer and Paas (1998) Cognitive architecture and instructional design
finding: Precursor of the worked-example effect: the goal-free effect. Giving a non-specific goal ('find all the angles you can') stops means-ends search and improved schema construction in many studies. The authors infer load differences from speed on practice problems, not from direct load measures.
numbers: Sweller, Mawer and Ward 1983 (kinematics, geometry, secondary students) and Owen and Sweller 1985 (trigonometry): goal-free groups better on conventional test problems. Ayres 1993: most errors on two-step geometry problems fall in the subgoal phase, fewer under goal-free. Vollmeyer, Burns and Holyoak 1996: means-ends analysis slowed learning in biology problems.
limits: Review of earlier work; no Ns in this paper.
agent_relevance: Two ways to cut search load: show the solution, or remove the target. Both are cheap prompt changes to test.

source: Sweller (2023) The development of cognitive load theory: replication crises and incorporation of other theories can lead to theory change
finding: Author's own history of failed replications of the worked-example effect. Algebra worked examples beat problem solving in repeated experiments. The same test with geometry and then kinematics (physics) examples found no effect, and the failures lasted several years. The cause: in geometry and physics, text refers to a diagram, so the learner must split attention and integrate. Physical integration restored the effect. Algebra examples do not need that, because two adjacent lines carry the step.
numbers: No new data. Cites Tarmizi and Sweller 1988 and Ward and Sweller 1990 for integrated vs split examples.
quote: We tried geometry problems and obtained no evidence of superiority when students studied worked examples instead of solving problems.
limits: Retrospective account by the theory's founder. It explains the failure after the fact. The split-attention fix is itself a theory-saving step, though later tests of integrated formats support it.
agent_relevance: A format check for stored examples: if the example needs the reader to look up a referent elsewhere, the benefit may vanish. Keep each step self-contained.

source: Sweller (2023) The development of cognitive load theory: replication crises and incorporation of other theories can lead to theory change
finding: The effect is bounded by element interactivity and learner expertise. Worked examples beat problem solving only for high element interactivity material. For low element interactivity material, and for more expert learners, problem solving is better or equal (reversed effect). The author argues the earlier mixed results were theory failures, not replication failures, because the variable was not controlled.
numbers: Cites Chen, Kalyuga and Sweller 2015, 2016a,b, 2017 and Kalyuga et al. 2001 for the reversal. Element interactivity cannot be measured exactly, only estimated (Chen et al. 2023).
limits: The claim 'not a replication failure' can look unfalsifiable if element interactivity is estimated after the result. The text says it can only be estimated.
agent_relevance: Gate for the schema: use stored solved cases on tasks that are new and multi-part for the agent; skip them on routine, low-step tasks. Needs a cheap complexity signal.

source: Sweller (2023) The development of cognitive load theory: replication crises and incorporation of other theories can lead to theory change
finding: Why example instruction beats discovery in schools: Geary's split between biologically primary knowledge (learned without teaching) and biologically secondary knowledge (school subjects, needs explicit teaching). The worked-example effect is cited as the case where randomised trials went against problem-based learning.
numbers: Cites worked-example RCTs: Cooper and Sweller 1987; Paas 1992; Paas and van Merrienboer 1994; Sweller and Cooper 1985.
limits: Theory framing; not a test. The author notes discovery supporters ran few randomised trials.
agent_relevance: For an agent, 'secondary' tasks (formal procedures) are the target of the library; open-ended or primary-like tasks may not gain.

source: Atkinson, Derry, Renkl and Wortham (2000) Learning from examples: instructional principles from the worked examples research
finding: History of the programme. Before the 1980s practice was held to be the way to learn problem solving. Sweller's group (Mawer, Owen, Sweller, Levine) found that practice pushed novices into trial and error. Worked examples paired with practice did better. Zhu and Simon (1987) ran the first and most cited classroom studies. Carroll (1994) and Ward and Sweller (1990) added classroom support.
numbers: Quote of the older belief: 'The best way to teach children how to solve problems is to give them lots of problems to solve' (Van Engen 1959). Chase and Simon (1973): 'practice is the major independent variable in the acquisition of skill'.
limits: Review, no effect sizes. Authors are partly in the worked-examples camp (Renkl is one).
agent_relevance: The same belief is common for agents: more attempts means better. This is the contrary view for novice states.

source: Atkinson, Derry, Renkl and Wortham (2000) Learning from examples: instructional principles from the worked examples research
finding: Places worked examples in a four-stage skill model (Anderson, Fincham and Douglass 1997, ACT-R): 1 solve by analogy to known examples; 2 build declarative rules; 3 smooth, fast, procedural performance; 4 retrieve solutions from many stored examples. Worked examples help most in stages 1 and 2. They are not the preferred method for stage 3, which needs practice.
numbers: Four overlapping stages; no numbers.
limits: Stage boundaries overlap and depend on how familiar a given problem is.
agent_relevance: A usable stage test for the library: new problem type means show examples; familiar type means plain practice or direct solve. Case retrieval at stage 4 is the end state.

source: Atkinson, Derry, Renkl and Wortham (2000) Learning from examples: instructional principles from the worked examples research
finding: Split-attention boundary, with the negative result. Tarmizi and Sweller (1988) Experiment 3 on circle geometry: worked-example pairs (first problem of each pair solved) gave no gain on any measure and were slower on posttest time. Experiments 4 and 5 integrated the text into the diagram and then beat conventional practice and split examples. Ward and Sweller (1990) replicated in physics (geometric optics) in classroom homework, in three long-term experiments.
numbers: Six pairs of problems; three-item posttest; measures: time to solution, strategy, errors, problems processed. Quote: 'the guidance provided by worked examples not only failed to facilitate subsequent performance, it actually retarded learning'.
limits: Reported through a review; exact means not given. Fixed study time in the learning phase.
agent_relevance: Confirms: a badly formatted example can be worse than none. Test with and without the example for each library format.

source: Atkinson, Derry, Renkl and Wortham (2000) Learning from examples: instructional principles from the worked examples research
finding: Subgoal labels in examples. Catrambone and Holyoak (1990): four Poisson-distribution worked examples with subgoal annotations vs none. Both groups did the same on similar items and most novel items. The labelled group did better on one novel transfer item. Across later studies a label helped even when its words carried little meaning, and visual separation of step groups worked as well as labels.
numbers: Six-item transfer test: 2 near items, 4 novel items. Advantage on one novel item only (1 of 4). Later series: Catrambone 1994a,b; 1995a,b; 1996; 1998.
quote: it is the presence of a label, not necessarily its semantic content, that influences subgoal formation
limits: Small effect in the founding study (one item). Later studies are reported without numbers in this review.
agent_relevance: Directly about the subgoal library: chunk the steps into labelled groups. The label may act by grouping, so the format of the grouping matters more than the wording.

source: Atkinson, Derry, Renkl and Wortham (2000) Learning from examples: instructional principles from the worked examples research
finding: Self-explanation. Chi et al. (1989) found that good learners studying physics examples explained unexplained steps, monitored accurately and referred back less. Renkl (1997b) found stable differences between learners, linked to how often they explained deep structure. A 15-minute training (rationale, modelled example, coached example) raised self-explanation by about two standard deviations and improved transfer.
numbers: Renkl, Stark, Gruber and Mandl (1998): explicit training effect about 2 SD on self-explanation activity; learning gain reliable; aptitude-treatment interaction on near transfer (low prior knowledge learners gained most).
limits: Learner-specific. The training study used a compound-interest domain. Review gives no Ns.
agent_relevance: An agent that reads a stored example should be made to explain why each step is taken. Self-explanation is the active part. Reading alone is weak.

source: Atkinson, Derry, Renkl and Wortham (2000) Learning from examples: instructional principles from the worked examples research
finding: Variability and sequencing. Paas and van Merrienboer (1994) crossed low vs high problem variability with worked vs practice instruction in geometry (four groups, six lesson problems, six-item transfer posttest). Worked examples gave a main effect and an interaction: variability only helped with worked examples. Trafton and Reiser (1993, LISP): example then matching practice problem alternated beat blocked examples then problems.
numbers: Paas and van Merrienboer: 4 groups; high variability = 2 problem subtypes, low = 1; no main effect of variability. Trafton and Reiser: 6 example-practice pairs, alternating faster and more accurate than blocked on three near-transfer items.
limits: Review, no Ns or means. The alternating result is read by Trafton and Reiser as support for knowledge compilation over example generalisation (two rival accounts).
agent_relevance: Vary the stored cases only if the agent studies them rather than solves. Put the matched try-it right after the example, not at the end of a batch.

source: Atkinson, Derry, Renkl and Wortham (2000) Learning from examples: instructional principles from the worked examples research
finding: Early evidence for fading and incomplete examples. Stark (1999) blanked parts of Renkl's examples and gave feedback on the learner's guesses. Incomplete examples cut ineffective self-explanations such as rereading and raised transfer. Paas (1992) had found no difference between incomplete and complete examples, but that was not his main aim.
numbers: No numbers in the review.
limits: Conflict between two studies, not resolved in the review.
agent_relevance: Supports blanking a step in a stored solution and asking the agent to supply it, then checking it.

source: Van Merrienboer and Paas (1990) Automation and schema acquisition in learning elementary computer programming: implications for the design of practice
finding: Programming-practice design paper that argues for putting useful worked examples directly beside practice. It describes Cooper and Sweller (1987): one group got a few illustrative examples then conventional problems; the other got each problem paired with an identical-format solved problem. The paired group had a shorter acquisition phase, fewer acquisition errors, and better near and far transfer. Also proposes completion assignments (partial program to finish).
numbers: Cooper and Sweller 1987 as described: shorter acquisition, fewer errors, better near and far transfer. Completion vs conventional assignments: higher program-construction scores (van Merrienboer in press; van Merrienboer and de Croock 1989). No Ns in this paper.
limits: Theory paper, no new data. Describes Cooper and Sweller secondhand.
agent_relevance: Pairing each task with a solved twin is the same as retrieving a solved neighbour at call time. Completion problems map to partial-plan prompts.

source: Renkl (2014) Toward an instructionally oriented theory of example-based learning (abstract, PubMed 24070563)
finding: Theory of example-based learning with descriptive and prescriptive parts. Descriptive: relevance and effectiveness of examples, phases of skill acquisition, learning processes. Prescriptive: instructional principles to exploit examples. Integrates worked examples, observational learning and analogical reasoning.
numbers: No numbers in abstract.
quote: Learning from examples is a very effective means of initial cognitive skill acquisition.
limits: Only the abstract page was read; full text not available this session.
agent_relevance: Three-part frame (examples, observation, analogy) fits a library plus retrieval plus analogical mapping design.

source: Hoogerheide and Roelle (2020) Example-based learning: new theoretical perspectives and use-inspired advances to a contemporary instructional approach
finding: Editorial that summarises where the field is. Worked examples alternated with practice are more effective and more efficient than unaided practice alone for novices. A comparison found no significant difference between worked and modelling examples on outcomes, effort or self-efficacy. Open questions: sequencing, long sequences (expertise reversal), analogical comparison of examples, learning from errors, individual differences.
numbers: Van Harsel et al. (2020) studied four sequences (examples only, problems only, example-problem pairs, problem-example pairs) with 4 tasks (Exp 1) or 8 tasks (Exp 2). Results are not given in the editorial.
limits: Editorial, not data. 'Effective and efficient' is cited from earlier primary studies.
agent_relevance: Efficiency (same score for less effort) is the usual result. For an agent that equals fewer tokens or fewer attempts at equal accuracy.

source: Schwonke, Renkl, Krieg, Wittwer, Aleven and Salden (2009) The worked-example effect: not an artefact of lousy control conditions (abstract page)
finding: Two experiments with Cognitive Tutor (algebra-type tutor with feedback and hints) vs a version with faded worked examples. Experiment 1: similar procedural skill and conceptual understanding in less learning time. Experiment 2: the efficiency gain replicated and conceptual understanding was deeper in the example group.
numbers: Per-condition Ns and means not available this session (abstract only).
limits: Only the abstract and portal summary were read. Reed et al. (2012), per a search snippet not opened, say the transfer advantage in Experiment 1 was not replicated in Experiment 2 or in Schwonke et al. (2011).
agent_relevance: Tests the effect against a strong scaffold, not against bare problem solving. This is the right baseline for our agent: the plain agent with hints and checks.

source: Sweller and Cooper (1985) The use of worked examples as a substitute for problem solving in learning algebra
finding: Founding study, five algebra experiments. Worked-example then problem pairs vs problems only. Worked-example group did better on similar post-test problems. Authors argued that search during problem solving does not direct attention to schemas.
numbers: Not read. A secondary web note (Wikipedia, not verified) says example learners took about half as long on a post-test and made about one fifth of the errors, and that the gain did not extend to varied post-test problems. Treat as unverified.
limits: Full text not accessible (publisher blocked). Numbers above are unconfirmed.
agent_relevance: The 'does not extend to varied problems' point is the transfer risk for any schema.

source: Cooper and Sweller (1987) Effects of schema acquisition and rule automation on mathematical problem-solving transfer
finding: Per a WorldCat abstract seen in a search result: schema acquisition precedes rule automation, schemas help similar problems, rule automation helps transfer to different problems, and worked examples help both.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Search snippet only. The secondhand account in van Merrienboer and Paas (1990) is the opened source for the design.
agent_relevance: Two separable gains: schema (recognise problem type) and automation (run the rule). A library gives the first; repetition gives the second.

source: Barbieri, Miller-Cotto, Clerjuste and Chawla (2023) A meta-analysis of the worked examples effect on mathematics performance
finding: Meta-analysis, robust variance estimation. Overall medium effect on mathematics performance. Studies with only correct examples had larger effects than only incorrect or mixed. Effect was medium for both practice and initial acquisition use.
numbers: Hedges g = 0.48, p = 0.01 (from a search summary; study count and CI not read).
limits: Paywalled; only a secondary summary was read. A university news item claims 100+ studies reviewed, unconfirmed.
agent_relevance: The best single effect-size anchor for the plan: about half a standard deviation in maths, with wide spread. Verify the figures before quoting.

source: Udvardi-Lakos, Weirich, Asbrand and Renkl (2024) Example-based learning in heuristic domains (abstract, PubMed 39377055)
finding: Worked examples in a heuristic (argumentation) skill domain. Using a relevant content domain in the examples did not reduce learning versus an irrelevant one, contrary to earlier advice to use simple, familiar content.
numbers: 142 psychology students; relevant vs irrelevant exemplifying domain; cognitive load, declarative knowledge, content knowledge and argumentation quality measured.
limits: Abstract only; heuristic domain, not a fixed procedure. Tests content choice, not the example vs problem contrast.
agent_relevance: For open-ended tasks the example content need not be toy content. Relevant cases are fine as stored examples.

source: Element interactivity and example-problem sequences (2020, Br J Educ Psychol, abstract, PubMed 31465546)
finding: Two experiments crossed sequence (worked example then problem vs problem then worked example) with element interactivity (low vs high). For high-interactivity material and novices, example-then-problem was better. For low-interactivity material and more knowledgeable learners, no difference.
numbers: Experiment 1: 52 Year-5 pupils (Indonesia). Experiment 2: 96 Year-8 pupils. 2 x 2 design with element interactivity repeated within subjects.
limits: Abstract only; means not read. Indonesian school samples, maths.
agent_relevance: Order rule: show the solved case first on hard items. On easy items the order does not matter, so skip the library.

source: Worked examples, cognitive aptitudes and the self-explanation mechanism: a replication (2026, Br J Educ Psychol, abstract, PubMed 42171417)
finding: A replication on whether self-explanation quality mediates the worked-example effect. The original found no mediation. The replication, with a stronger method, did: the indirect effect through self-explanation was stronger for lower prior knowledge and lower working memory. Shifting ability moderated the effect directly (bigger benefit at lower ability) with no mediation. Fluid intelligence did not moderate.
numbers: 115 university students, six ill-defined statistics problems with or without worked examples. Self-explanation coded as use of case information to justify statistical claims.
limits: Abstract only; effect sizes not read. Ill-defined statistics problems, university sample.
agent_relevance: The benefit runs partly through the learner explaining the example. For an agent, force a case-specific justification of each step.

source: Does working memory moderate the effect of fading on math performance? (2025, Br J Educ Psychol, abstract, PubMed 40329570)
finding: Four conditions on 6th-grade geometry homework: worked examples with self-explanation prompts, fading with prompts, fading alone, problem solving only. Posttest differed by condition. Fading had the largest pre-to-post effect sizes. Only prior knowledge moderated the fading effect, not working memory.
numbers: N = 114, 3 days of intervention on ASSISTments, pre and post test.
limits: Abstract only; fading beat full worked examples here. Effect sizes not read.
agent_relevance: Fading (remove steps over time) beat plain examples here. Supports a schedule that withdraws library support as the agent succeeds.

source: Performance expectancies moderate the effectiveness of more or less generative activities over time (2019, Front Psychol, abstract, PubMed 31496963)
finding: Boundary on timing. Eighth graders (linear functions) did problem solving or reduced-self-explanation worked examples. Immediately, problem solving was better for high-expectancy pupils; no difference for low. After 3 months it reversed for low-expectancy pupils (problem solving better). Problem-solving advantage for high-expectancy pupils faded over 3 months while the worked-example group held steady.
numbers: Sample of eighth graders in an advanced track (N not given in abstract); immediate test and delayed test after 3 months.
limits: Abstract only. The comparison group was a worked-example type designed to reduce self-explanation, which is a weak version.
agent_relevance: Short-run and long-run results can disagree. A test of the library should include a delayed check, not just the immediate score.

source: Effects of example-free instruction and worked examples on problem-solving (2021, Heliyon, abstract, PubMed 34458621)
finding: A counter-result. For critical-thinking problems, instruction without examples gave better problem solving than worked examples that had no instructional explanation. Learners also reported more efficient processing after the explanation.
numbers: n = 32 university students in South Korea.
limits: Very small sample; abstract only; worked examples had no explanation text, which differs from usual designs.
agent_relevance: An example with no stated reason for each step may be worse than a plain statement of the rule. Store the why with the how.
